title: Dimension‐Specific Attentional Sensitivity in Fears of Compassion: A Dot‐Probe Investigation of Three Dimensions
abstract: ABSTRACT The three dimensions of fears of compassion (FoC)—fear of being compassionate to oneself (FoC self ), of receiving compassion from others (FoS from ), and of expressing compassion to others (FoC others )—have been linked to a range of psychopathological outcomes, yet little is known about whether these fears are reflected in early attentional processing of socio‐emotional cues. Using a dot‐probe paradigm with positive and negative emotional faces, the present study examined dimension‐specific attentional patterns in Chinese university students. Adopting the evolutionary‐motivational framework of compassion, and following recommendations to analyze the three Fear of Conpassion Scale subscales separately rather than as a composite, participants were classified into high and low groups separately on each subscale, and three parallel linear mixed models were fitted with gender as a covariate. Across all three models, high‐FoC participants responded approximately 50–65 ms more slowly than low‐FoC participants, with the largest group difference observed for FoC from . Significant Group × Congruence interactions emerged for the two interpersonal dimensions (FoC from and FoC others ) and a marginal interaction for FoC self , with a consistent descriptive pattern across dimensions: high‐FoC groups displayed a vigilance‐like congruence effect on negative‐face trials whereas low‐FoC groups showed a negligible effect. The three‐way Group × Emotion × Congruence interaction was not significant in any model, and the present design was not powered to detect such higher‐order effects. Findings are therefore interpreted as preliminary evidence that fear of compassion—particularly from others—is associated with a subtle attentional sensitivity to the location of negative facial cues, consistent with attachment‐based accounts of FoC. Adequately powered confirmatory replication is required.
